Hi [~accountid:610a3ee66051c5006aeeeea1],

From my research, this giveaway thing has a bit of complexity.

From a tax perspective, Ley del Juego (law of the games and giveaways) says: _The passive subjects as taxpayers will be natural persons, legal entities or entities included in section 4 of article 35 of Law 58/2003, of December 17, General Tax that operate, organize or develop the activities taxed by this tax._

(the percentage of the tax is 10% and Bolt as the organiser would have to fill in modelo 685 and pay the tax to the Spanish HMRC)

If the value of the prize is above EUR 300 the winner will have to declare it in his self assessment and the organizers (Bolt) will be obliged to set up the withholdings corresponding to the winners, when the prizes that have corresponded to them individually exceed the value of €300. 

From a GDPR perspective, we should be registered with Agencia Espanola de Proteccion de Datos.

And we also must comply with the legal policy of the corresponding network. The different social networks have different rules to comply with.

Is there a legal advisor dedicated to Marketing things? If not, and considering that the Marketing team is very likely to promote these types of initiatives in the future, it may be worth investing a little resources in this matter and creating a kind of playbook. 



Let’s discuss it later\! Thank you\!

Hello Richard, 

I hope you are well. The applicable legislation doesn't stipulate an explicit requirement on using BankID so I cannot say that it would be unlawful not to. Obviously, from an evidence perspective, it puts us in a less favourable position if the account owner doesn't have to authenticate himself with BankID. Case law in Sweden has stipulated that when a user authenticates himself/herself with BankID, it is on the user to prove that the authentication was unauthorised/incorrect and not the other way around.

What I'm trying to say is that if we allow users to book vehicles without proper authentication (meeting the requirement of advanced electronic signature, e.g. BankID) and it turns out that someone unauthorised has used an account to book a vehicle, it will be quite difficult for us to argue that we have checked the correct persons driver’s license before handing over the vehicle.

Best regards,  

Erik

+*External counsel analysis:*+

# +*Using of dashcams in Germany*+

In the opinion of the data protection supervisory authorities of the German states (including the Data Protection Conference - the joint body of the data protection supervisory authorities in Germany), the use of dashcams in Germany is generally not permitted. The authorities justify their view with the argument that by using a dashcam, third parties in public space would be recorded at the same time, which cannot be justified via Art. 6 (1) lit. f GDPR: Because there would be a permanent, unsolicited recording of traffic events as well as an unsolicited recording of mostly uninvolved traffic participants which would affect these persons in their rights of Art. 8 of the Fundamental Rights Charter. Furthermore, it has to be considered that - according to opinion of the authorities - third parties usually have no possibility to take knowledge of such recording and therefore cannot take action against it or to object (comp. “Position paper on the inadmissibility of video surveillance by vehicles - dashcams).

However, the German Federal Court of Justice (“BGH”) has decided that - within narrow limits - the use of dashcam recordings for evidence purposes in connection with accidents, etc. is permissible. The requirements are high. In this respect, the Federal Court of Justice considers the storage of dashcam-recordings over a period of 4 hours to be inadmissible (comp. BGH, decision from 15.5.2018, Az.: VI ZR 233/17; ZD 2018, 422).  The BGH demands technical measures to protect privacy, such as (i) very short storage periods of the records, (ii) short-term, occasion-based recordings which are only activated by a motion sensor in the event of a collision or severe slow-down of the vehicle, (iii) pixelation of persons or (iv) automatic deletion outside the control of the dashcam user. 

*Please note that this statement by the BGH only applies to the use of dashcams for evidence purposes in the event of accidents. In all other situations, the use of dashcams - in accordance with the opinion of the data protection authorities - is generally classified as unlawful.*

In the literature, solutions are proposed taking into account the BGH decision, according to which the *maximum recording duration is limited to a short period of time - e. g. 60 seconds - and the recording is overwritten again, provided that no accident has occurred* (comp. Prof. Dr. Schröder – “data protection when using cameras in automobiles; ZD 2021, 302). With regard to the information obligations towards data subjects, the literature argues that this would require disproportionate efforts and is therefore not necessary as stipulated by Art. 14 (5) GDPR.

In a nutshell: Dashcams may currently only be used in Germany if the above-mentioned measures are implemented, in particular, very short recording / deletion times of max. +60sec to 120sec+ are observed. 

+To your questions raised within your E-Mail:+

# _What are the requirements for the use of dashboard cameras in Germany? Can the regulatory approach vary depending on a federal state?_

Answer: Regarding the requirements, please see above. There is a general approach of all German Data Protection Authorities in the different federal states streamlined by the Data Protection Conference - the joint body of the data protection supervisory authorities in Germany.

# _What practical measures should be implemented to proceed with using dash cameras in Germany in a compliant manner? What are recommended practices in terms of handling the recordings?_

Answer: The measures mentioned above have to be implemented for a compliant usage of dashcams which requires in particular very short recording / deletion times all +60sec to 120sec+. 

# +*Speed tracking + notification Service*+

Speed-tracking and speed-notifications are in general not subject to any other local restrictions under data protection law besides those of the GDPR. This type of service can be designed either via consent (opt-in) or as a service via Art. 6 (1) lit. b GDPR. A general collection / monitoring of speed in the context of legitimate interests (Art. 6 (1) lit. f GDPR) - i.e. without consent or a respective agreement with the data subject - is not possible in this context. In the area of employment law, further requirements may arise via Art. 88 GDPR in conjunction with Section 26 BDSG, but the respective employer would be responsible for this.

Wrapping up where to we managed to get this time and what’s next, especially what [~accountid:5a2fdc90a761683f858edf19] said about starting from a Refund Strategy.

*What we know today?*

If Bolt user (rider/eater/passenger) did not get the service (missing food / messed-up food / cold and unedible food / driver not showed up / cancelled mid-way / car broke-down / etc.) → Users are generally entitled for a refund (food + delivery price; rental fee; fare).

All the legal arguments about who is service provider (restaurant? courier? driver?) and Bolt is a platform - aside, if User is such cases would turn to its credit-card issuing bank and claim chargeback → unless we put a good file together proving that User properly received full service, chargeback will be authorised. Which means that User will get money back to his credit card, and liability to cover this will trickle down from acquirer on our side - through the Payment Partners we use - and onto us. 

Me and [~accountid:624469dd45ece00069c967bd]  are looking deeper to understand how chargeback process plays out in our case still. 

But bottom line is clear: _in cases where there is a good doubt if User actually properly received service, our failure to satisfy User’s request - would most likely result in a chargeback thus Bolt still paying up + incurring chargeback fee (aka paying more in the end)._

*What we need to do in such cases?*

When we deal with such User complaints and determine that a “refund” is due to a client - we should follow the Refund Rules:

*Rule 1: Validate with a user where the Refund should go to:*

* Back to the original payment method (aka CC)
* OR Bolt Balance is OK

*Rule 2: Always follow User preference*

* if requested back to the original payment method - this is what we need to do
** also in cases where we think a partial refund is only due → we should refund full amount (as cannot refund partial only

Full Policy here (repeated from last post): 

!Screenshot 2022-06-01 at 14.37.43 (3d2e1842-e02d-456e-b197-d08cd58f6ea1).png|width=528,height=644!

*How to determine as Refund that needs to follow above OR something else and thus deserves a separate treatment?*

As per [~accountid:5a2fdc90a761683f858edf19] 's post below - we need a full high level policy how we deal with refunds and work from there to determine how much risk and where we want to accept, how to optimally use Bolt Balance, etc.

So for now advice / guidance is that:

* in situation we  promised product/service not received, then there are grounds for chargeback → Thus we are better off following above refund process.
* in situations where complaint is about service quality more than anything else and we have data points to prove that service was actually delivered and the complaint is related to non-satisfaction more than with lack of service → issuing tokens of “appreciation” instead of refunds is a good choise.

We should reopen this and develop legal guidance much more granular level per-vertical once we have a general refund policy and decision on how / were use BB. So leave it with [~accountid:5a2fdc90a761683f858edf19] to involve legal into this going process.

Hey,

it does not say to refund the unknown charge. It just says to check whether the user is enrolled into the Bolt Balance flow or not. If they are, we shouldn’t mark the payment as fraudulent (nothing bad will happen, but you’ll just see an error). There’s also an explaining paragraph about it below:

*_Why don't we mark the payment as fraudulent if the partial refund option is available?_*

_Blocking/marking the payment as fraudulent is not the best solution for these cases. At the moment, the Fraud team is working on a better solution for this and once it is done, we will review the process and make necessary changes. For now, please follow the procedure and do not worry about not marking the payment as fraudulent (if it is specified in the process that this should not be done)._

If the unknown charge comes from a Bolt Balance top up, the process is this:

* _Open the related user’s profile_
* _Choose User(s) blocking option and click Block users & related devices/cards_
* _Add a comment with the ZD ticket link and a short description on the profile_
* _Inform the reporter that we have taken internal measures regarding this issue (do not disclose what exactly)_

----

The process doesn’t mention anything about refunding these charges. Additionally, we’ve _even stated that we should not refund them:_

_Marking the payment as fraudulent does not refund it to the customer. Please note that we don't refund unknown charges. If the customer asks how they can get their money back,_ *_do not advise them to do a chargeback, but advise them to contact their bank for further information._*

----

In this situation the Passenger is considered as a separate data controller where they make a decision to further publish/share any personal data. There is no such restrictions in our T&C-s or Privacy Notice for Passengers which would give us a ground to act further.

Turns out the labor law in NO is quite strict on hiring temporary staff from temporary-work agencies, see the description below:

“If a person is to be employed temporarily, one or more of the following conditions must be present:

* When the work is of a temporary nature. Examples are seasonal work and project work. +The ordinary day-to-day tasks of the undertaking are not to be performed by temporary employees.+
* Work as a trainee. This is employment designed to provide training or qualifications in a field, and must involve a training situation beyond that which is normal for performance of the duties of the post.
* Work as a temporary replacement for another person or persons. This must involve a genuine replacement situation, e.g. replacement of a person on sick leave or in connection with other leave or holiday.
* Participants in labour market schemes under the auspices of or in cooperation with the Labour and Welfare Service.
* Certain posts in sports - athletes, trainers, referees and other leaders within organised sports.”

Hi everyone, as promised previously, additional updates regarding early cashout and driver debt relationship is here~Working document:

[spreadsheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/18JO6rFZBNNCt7FWhmPNNNOYzwgLJ-yTm9SR-P0vFJjw/edit?usp=sharing]I'm looking at the proportion of cash-blocked drivers that use early cashout, by week, before the blocking date. By framing the analysis as a cohort analysis, we can see the shift in driver behavior per month, and see the extent of early cashout usage prior to blocking date.*Calculation Illustration*


For example, let's say there is 100 drivers that got blocked in Jan 2022. Out of 100 drivers, only 20 of them use early cashout in a week before the blocking date, so the *_one prior week usage rate is 20%._* If there are 15 drivers out of 100 that use early cashout during the second week prior the blocking date, *_the two prior week usage rate is 15%._**Sample Used in this Analysis*


To correctly identify the drivers of interest, we only select drivers that are already blocked since before 20th of June, under the assumption that they do not take any activities to unblock themselves for a month. This group of drivers is the drivers that "churned" from Bolt and has the potential to abuse early cashout feature and accumulate debt.*Insights*

* In GE : Number of cash-blocked drivers per month is few, ranging from 3 to 17. From June 2021 to Feb 2022, almost all of the blocked drivers never use early cashout. However, in April and June 2022, more than half of the blocked drivers use early cashout in a week before they are blocked (*_one prior week usage rate > 50%_*). This cohort of drivers also show high adoption of early cashout, with >20% of them use early cashout since 5 weeks prior to their cash-blocking date.
* In KE : Majority of blocked drivers do not use early cashout. During Oct-Dec 2021, there was a spike in *_one prior week usage rate_*, from < 3.5% to 8 - 14%. The normal rate for KE is < 5%. However, the difference between one prior week usage rate and two prior week usage rate is huge during the spike months, indicating that drivers adopt early cashout just before the blocking event.
* In GH : There was a huge spike in *_one prior week usage rate_* in aug 2021 (72%), while the two prior week and three prior week usage rate are only 29% and 24% in that cohort. Maybe something happened in August? The *_one prior week usage rate_* in GH declined from 72% in August 2021, to 48% in Sept 2021, to 31% in Oct 2021, to 28% in Nov 2021, and now the rate is pretty constant around 7-8% since March 2022.
* In ZA : Relatively low *_one prior week usage rate_* (< 5%). Spike in the metric happened during Oct-Dec 2021. However, the churned drivers also use early cashout since weeks before they are blocked.
* In NG : Similar pattern with Kenya, but the spike occurred in Aug-Oct 2021 instead of Oct-Dec. The *_one prior week usage rate_* in the last several months is very low (< 3%). However, it seems the drivers that churned during those cohorts also use early cashout since weeks before they are blocked, indicating that the drivers do not use early cashout for the sole reason of accumulating debt.
* In TZ : Very low *_one prior week usage rate_* (<3%).

*WiP*

+*Project Goal/s*+

# Course to cover both hard and soft skills needed for TLs that were not included previously
# More product-specific information and tasks to allow new TLs an opportunity to practice
# Course to be updated and owned by L&D
# Regular tracking of performance, challenges and feedback from new TLs
# TLs are better prepared for the role with the addition of practical tasks and topics
# A clear understanding of how to work with OS suppliers

+*What actually happened?*+

While the course was designed as a 5-day course, it was found that it’s to complete in a shorter time. This is based on only 1 learner and that learner is part of the safety team (the safety team has a different onboarding course but has the majority of the same topics and assignments as the CS TL onboarding course). However, what would need to be stressed is that it would need to be completed in 5 working days. This would need to be understood by both the new TL and their STL. 


Tereza created a similar [KPI tracker sheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FkViAjRmB77QAqQR6Du-yFyes2RPxfE3CGY7nK8JZbA/edit#gid=100051123] that’s used for the FD agent onboarding. This wasn’t done before, not allowing us to understand the TL onboarding experience. 

With TL onboarding, previously, workshops were hosted by either an STL or another experienced TL. However, there was limited information as to if and when these took place. Now, instructions have been added to the STL Confluence page on how to use ILT within TB. This way, we can see who hosted the session and when. We can then draw feedback from the TL and host on the workshop experience. 

With a hiring freeze, we don’t expect any new TLs to go through the course anytime soon. meaning that updates or any changes required may not readily be available. We should just keep an eye on what’s being communicated, and when needed, ask questions, and be curious whether the update or change would impact the course or further enhance it.

For now, we did not go into product-line specifics, but rather somewhat general for now. The reason for this is for TLs to go through the course and evaluate feedback. But this does not mean that we can’t add it later. If so, we would require some support from STLs as to what assignments can be added.

The layout of the course is more structured. For example, we included estimated unit completion times so the TL can plan their day accordingly. We also relied heavily on using [Figma documents|https://www.figma.com/file/5upqz8uWCb72pBfLLCvP5j/TL-Onboarding-Revamp?node-id=4%3A2] instead of long videos. These are easier to change or update and the onboarding content is accessible to L&D leads.

The time frame for completion was surprisingly adequate. I’d say the reason for this was that it wasn’t an individual effort but teamwork that helped us reach our deadline. As mentioned earlier, due to a hiring freeze, we have not had anyone go through the course so it is not possible to report on any metric successes. 

*What went well:*

I’d say that the way we organized ourselves in terms of who will concentrate on what task worked really well. Several TLs and STLs recognized that a change was needed and some volunteered or offered their assistance without hesitation. With stakeholders, the communication was more than satisfactory and allowed us to draw as much info as we needed. In some situations, certain stakeholders were either wrapped up or completing their changes for their respective departments, for example, the DEI report was published very early in the year, and the recruitment team made some changes in the way TLs should request Workday changes, etc.

*What didn’t go well:*

Firstly, not having any learners take the training to build a conclusive report on whether it was successful or not. We did not focus too much on product specifics and went with a more universal approach for leads. In some cases, it was hard to get a response or face time with certain stakeholders. So it was more of a waiting game.

*How to avoid this?*

I’d say be a bit more persuasive towards certain stakeholders and paint a picture that is specifically fine-tuned to what’s needed from them than rather sending them the full plan. 

*What else can be improved?*

Maintaining and/or expanding on collaborators in the event we open hiring again. This way we won’t have to hunt for additional support where needed. Continue to ask for areas where there are gaps currently and try to implement this into the onboarding.
